days.rawContent:
# Day 39: RDS and Managed Databases
[← Previous Day](../day-38-s3-buckets/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-40-three-tier-vpc/README.md)

## Goal
Provision, secure, and inspect a managed relational database using Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS), DB Subnet Groups, and least-privilege security groups in an isolated private tier.

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 90 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [Amazon RDS User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/) — Official documentation covering supported engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL), DB instance classes (`db.t3.micro`), DB Subnet Groups, and Multi-AZ replication.
- 📖 [Amazon RDS Security Best Practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/CHAP_BestPractices.Security.html) — AWS guide on VPC isolation, disabling public accessibility, encryption at rest, and credential management.

## Do
In this lab, you will create a multi-AZ private network foundation, create an RDS DB Subnet Group, launch a free-tier eligible PostgreSQL instance without public accessibility, and retrieve connection details via the AWS CLI.

1. **Create a VPC and two private subnets across two distinct Availability Zones**:
   AWS RDS requires a DB Subnet Group containing subnets in at least two different Availability Zones for high availability failover readiness.
   ```bash
   REGION="us-east-1"
   VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 create-vpc \
     --region "${REGION}" \
     --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 \
     --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=vpc,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=day39-db-vpc}]' \
     --query "Vpc.VpcId" \
     --output text)

   SUBNET_1=$(aws ec2 create-subnet \
     --region "${REGION}" \
     --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" \
     --cidr-block 10.0.10.0/24 \
     --availability-zone "${REGION}a" \
     --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=day39-priv-subnet-1a}]' \
     --query "Subnet.SubnetId" \
     --output text)

   SUBNET_2=$(aws ec2 create-subnet \
     --region "${REGION}" \
     --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" \
     --cidr-block 10.0.20.0/24 \
     --availability-zone "${REGION}b" \
     --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=day39-priv-subnet-1b}]' \
     --query "Subnet.SubnetId" \
     --output text)

   echo "VPC: ${VPC_ID} | Subnets: ${SUBNET_1}, ${SUBNET_2}"
   ```

2. **Create an RDS DB Subnet Group**:
   ```bash
   aws rds create-db-subnet-group \
     --region "${REGION}" \
     --db-subnet-group-name "day39-db-subnet-group" \
     --db-subnet-group-description "Private subnet group for day 39 RDS lab" \
     --subnet-ids "${SUBNET_1}" "${SUBNET_2}"
   ```

3. **Create Security Groups for Application and Database**:
   ```bash
   # Application SG
   APP_SG=$(aws ec2 create-security-group \
     --region "${REGION}" \
     --group-name "day39-app-sg" \
     --description "App server security group" \
     --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" \
     --query "GroupId" \
     --output text)

   # Database SG
   DB_SG=$(aws ec2 create-security-group \
     --region "${REGION}" \
     --group-name "day39-rds-sg" \
     --description "RDS PostgreSQL security group" \
     --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" \
     --query "GroupId" \
     --output text)

   # Allow PostgreSQL port 5432 exclusively from the APP_SG
   aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
     --region "${REGION}" \
     --group-id "${DB_SG}" \
     --protocol tcp \
     --port 5432 \
     --source-group "${APP_SG}"

   echo "App SG: ${APP_SG} | DB SG: ${DB_SG}"
   ```

4. **Launch a Free-Tier Eligible RDS PostgreSQL Instance**:
   We will deploy a Single-AZ `db.t3.micro` instance with 20 GiB storage, auto-minor-version-upgrade enabled, and public access disabled.
   ```bash
   DB_IDENTIFIER="day39-postgres-db"
   DB_PASSWORD="CloudEngLab2026Password!"

   aws rds create-db-instance \
     --region "${REGION}" \
     --db-instance-identifier "${DB_IDENTIFIER}" \
     --db-instance-class db.t3.micro \
     --engine postgres \
     --allocated-storage 20 \
     --master-username "cloudadmin" \
     --master-user-password "${DB_PASSWORD}" \
     --db-subnet-group-name "day39-db-subnet-group" \
     --vpc-security-group-ids "${DB_SG}" \
     --no-publicly-accessible \
     --backup-retention-period 0 \
     --tags Key=Name,Value=day39-postgres-db
   ```

5. **Wait for DB instance availability and inspect connection endpoint**:
   RDS provisioning typically takes 5 to 10 minutes while AWS configures underlying compute and storage volumes.
   ```bash
   echo "Waiting for RDS instance to become available (this takes a few minutes)..."
   aws rds wait db-instance-available \
     --region "${REGION}" \
     --db-instance-identifier "${DB_IDENTIFIER}"

   # Retrieve DB endpoint and status
   aws rds describe-db-instances \
     --region "${REGION}" \
     --db-instance-identifier "${DB_IDENTIFIER}" \
     --query "DBInstances[0].[DBInstanceIdentifier,DBInstanceStatus,Endpoint.Address,Endpoint.Port,PubliclyAccessible]" \
     --output table
   ```

## Done When
- [ ] DB Subnet Group `day39-db-subnet-group` references subnets in at least two Availability Zones.
- [ ] Database Security Group allows ingress port 5432 strictly from `day39-app-sg`.
- [ ] RDS instance reaches status `available`.
- [ ] `PubliclyAccessible` is verified as `false` in `describe-db-instances`.
- [ ] Private endpoint DNS address (e.g. `day39-postgres-db.c...rds.amazonaws.com`) is recorded.

## Cost and Cleanup
Expected Cost: **$0.00** — The AWS Free Tier provides 750 hours/month of Single-AZ `db.t3.micro` (or `db.t4g.micro`) and 20 GB of General Purpose SSD storage for the first 12 months.

RDS instances incur hourly charges if left running outside the Free Tier. Always delete testing databases immediately after verifying:
```bash
REGION="us-east-1"
DB_IDENTIFIER="day39-postgres-db"

# 1. Delete RDS instance without creating a final snapshot
echo "Deleting RDS instance ${DB_IDENTIFIER}..."
aws rds delete-db-instance \
  --region "${REGION}" \
  --db-instance-identifier "${DB_IDENTIFIER}" \
  --skip-final-snapshot \
  --delete-automated-backups

echo "Waiting for RDS instance deletion..."
aws rds wait db-instance-deleted \
  --region "${REGION}" \
  --db-instance-identifier "${DB_IDENTIFIER}"

# 2. Delete DB Subnet Group
aws rds delete-db-subnet-group \
  --region "${REGION}" \
  --db-subnet-group-name "day39-db-subnet-group"

# 3. Delete Security Groups
aws ec2 delete-security-group --region "${REGION}" --group-id "${DB_SG}"
aws ec2 delete-security-group --region "${REGION}" --group-id "${APP_SG}"

# 4. Delete Subnets and VPC
aws ec2 delete-subnet --region "${REGION}" --subnet-id "${SUBNET_1}"
aws ec2 delete-subnet --region "${REGION}" --subnet-id "${SUBNET_2}"
aws ec2 delete-vpc --region "${REGION}" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}"

echo "All database and networking resources cleaned up successfully."
```

## Azure / GCP Equivalents
| AWS RDS Feature | Azure Equivalent | GCP Cloud SQL |
|-----------------|------------------|---------------|
| Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL/MySQL) | Azure Database for PostgreSQL / Azure SQL | Google Cloud SQL (PostgreSQL/MySQL) |
| DB Subnet Group | VNet Integration / Private Endpoint | Private Service Connect / VPC Peering |
| Multi-AZ (Standby Failover) | Zone-Redundant High Availability | High Availability (HA) Regional Configuration |
| Read Replica | Azure Read Replica | Cloud SQL Read Replica |
| Automated Snapshots | Automated Backups (LRS/GRS) | Cloud SQL Automated Backups |

- 📖 [Azure Database for PostgreSQL Documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/postgresql/)
- 📖 [Google Cloud SQL Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs)

## Stretch Goal
Understand High Availability: Contrast Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployments with Read Replicas. Multi-AZ provides synchronous replication to a standby instance in another AZ for automatic disaster failover (no read scaling), whereas Read Replicas use asynchronous replication for scaling read-heavy queries. Document the difference in recovery point objective (RPO) and recovery time objective (RTO).

## Common Mistakes
- **Failing to span at least two AZs in DB Subnet Group**: AWS requires at least two Availability Zones in a DB Subnet Group even for Single-AZ instances, ensuring the subnet group is ready if you decide to modify the instance to Multi-AZ later.
- **Enabling Public Accessibility**: Setting `--publicly-accessible` exposes your database port to the entire internet. Production databases should always reside in private subnets with private endpoints.
- **Forgetting `--skip-final-snapshot` during cleanup**: Forgetting `--skip-final-snapshot` triggers an unneeded snapshot creation before deletion, which delays teardown and incurs lingering snapshot storage costs.

days.title: Build a Three-Tier VPC Architecture
days.goal: Design and construct an enterprise-grade, highly available Three-Tier VPC architecture with public web subnets, private application subnets, and isolated private database subnets across multiple Availability Zones using the AWS CLI.
checklist: 6 subnets created across two Availability Zones (`us-east-1a` and `us-east-1b`).
Internet Gateway attached to VPC and linked to public subnets via `public-rt`.
NAT Gateway provisioned in a public subnet with an allocated Elastic IP.
App subnets associated with `app-tier-rt` pointing `0.0.0.0/0` to the NAT Gateway.
DB subnets associated with `db-tier-isolated-rt` containing only local VPC routing.
Security group chaining verified: Internet -> `ALB_SG` -> `APP_SG` -> `DB_SG`.

# Day 40: Build a Three-Tier VPC Architecture
[← Previous Day](../day-39-rds-databases/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-41-what-are-containers/README.md)

## Goal
Design and construct an enterprise-grade, highly available Three-Tier VPC architecture with public web subnets, private application subnets, and isolated private database subnets across multiple Availability Zones using the AWS CLI.

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 120 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [Amazon VPC Architecture: Scenario with Public and Private Subnets](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/VPC_Scenario2.html) — Official AWS reference architecture for multi-tier network segmentation and NAT routing.
- 📖 [AWS Well-Architected Framework: Reliability Pillar](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/welcome.html) — Architectural principles for multi-AZ fault tolerance and network boundary isolation.

## Do
In this milestone capstone lab for Module 5, you will construct a full Three-Tier VPC architecture across two Availability Zones (`us-east-1a` and `us-east-1b`):
- **Tier 1 (Public)**: 2 Public subnets with Internet Gateway for Load Balancers and NAT Gateways.
- **Tier 2 (Private App)**: 2 Private subnets routing egress traffic through a NAT Gateway for application servers.
- **Tier 3 (Private DB)**: 2 Isolated private subnets without internet access for backend databases.
- **Tiered Security Groups**: ALB SG -> App SG -> DB SG.

```
                    Internet
                       │
               [Internet Gateway]
                       │
  ┌────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Tier 1: Public Subnets (AZ-a & AZ-b)                │
  │   - Public Route Table (0.0.0.0/0 -> IGW)           │
  │   - [Application Load Balancer]  [NAT Gateway]      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────┘
                                         │
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────┐
  │ Tier 2: Private Application Subnets (AZ-a & AZ-b)   │
  │   - App Route Table (0.0.0.0/0 -> NAT Gateway)      │
  │   - [EC2 App Instances] (App SG)                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────┘
                                         │ (Local only)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────┐
  │ Tier 3: Isolated Database Subnets (AZ-a & AZ-b)     │
  │   - DB Route Table (Local VPC routing only)         │
  │   - [Amazon RDS Database] (DB SG)                   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

1. **Create the VPC and enable DNS hostnames**:
   ```bash
   REGION="us-east-1"
   VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 create-vpc \
     --region "${REGION}" \
     --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16 \
     --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=vpc,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=three-tier-production-vpc}]' \
     --query "Vpc.VpcId" \
     --output text)

   aws ec2 modify-vpc-attribute --region "${REGION}" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --enable-dns-hostnames '{"Value":true}'
   aws ec2 modify-vpc-attribute --region "${REGION}" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --enable-dns-support '{"Value":true}'
   echo "VPC: ${VPC_ID}"
   ```

2. **Create subnets across 2 Availability Zones (6 subnets total)**:
   ```bash
   # Tier 1: Public Subnets
   PUB_SUB_A=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --region "${REGION}" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 --availability-zone "${REGION}a" --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=pub-tier-1a}]' --query "Subnet.SubnetId" --output text)
   PUB_SUB_B=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --region "${REGION}" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --cidr-block 10.0.2.0/24 --availability-zone "${REGION}b" --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=pub-tier-1b}]' --query "Subnet.SubnetId" --output text)
   aws ec2 modify-subnet-attribute --region "${REGION}" --subnet-id "${PUB_SUB_A}" --map-public-ip-on-launch
   aws ec2 modify-subnet-attribute --region "${REGION}" --subnet-id "${PUB_SUB_B}" --map-public-ip-on-launch

   # Tier 2: Private Application Subnets
   APP_SUB_A=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --region "${REGION}" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --cidr-block 10.0.11.0/24 --availability-zone "${REGION}a" --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=app-tier-1a}]' --query "Subnet.SubnetId" --output text)
   APP_SUB_B=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --region "${REGION}" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --cidr-block 10.0.12.0/24 --availability-zone "${REGION}b" --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=app-tier-1b}]' --query "Subnet.SubnetId" --output text)

   # Tier 3: Isolated Database Subnets
   DB_SUB_A=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --region "${REGION}" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --cidr-block 10.0.21.0/24 --availability-zone "${REGION}a" --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=db-tier-1a}]' --query "Subnet.SubnetId" --output text)
   DB_SUB_B=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --region "${REGION}" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --cidr-block 10.0.22.0/24 --availability-zone "${REGION}b" --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=db-tier-1b}]' --query "Subnet.SubnetId" --output text)

   echo "Subnets created: Public (${PUB_SUB_A}, ${PUB_SUB_B}), App (${APP_SUB_A}, ${APP_SUB_B}), DB (${DB_SUB_A}, ${DB_SUB_B})"
   ```

3. **Deploy Internet Gateway and Public Route Table**:
   ```bash
   IGW_ID=$(aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --region "${REGION}" --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=internet-gateway,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=three-tier-igw}]' --query "InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId" --output text)
   aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --region "${REGION}" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --internet-gateway-id "${IGW_ID}"

   PUB_RT=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --region "${REGION}" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=route-table,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=public-rt}]' --query "RouteTable.RouteTableId" --output text)
   aws ec2 create-route --region "${REGION}" --route-table-id "${PUB_RT}" --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id "${IGW_ID}"

   aws ec2 associate-route-table --region "${REGION}" --subnet-id "${PUB_SUB_A}" --route-table-id "${PUB_RT}"
   aws ec2 associate-route-table --region "${REGION}" --subnet-id "${PUB_SUB_B}" --route-table-id "${PUB_RT}"
   ```

4. **Deploy NAT Gateway for Private App Tier Outbound Egress**:
   Allocate an Elastic IP and create the NAT Gateway in the public subnet `PUB_SUB_A`:
   ```bash
   EIP_ALLOC_ID=$(aws ec2 allocate-address --region "${REGION}" --domain vpc --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=elastic-ip,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=nat-gw-eip}]' --query "AllocationId" --output text)

   NAT_GW_ID=$(aws ec2 create-nat-gateway --region "${REGION}" --subnet-id "${PUB_SUB_A}" --allocation-id "${EIP_ALLOC_ID}" --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=natgateway,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=three-tier-nat-gw}]' --query "NatGateway.NatGatewayId" --output text)

   echo "Waiting for NAT Gateway ${NAT_GW_ID} to become available (takes ~2 minutes)..."
   aws ec2 wait nat-gateway-available --region "${REGION}" --nat-gateway-ids "${NAT_GW_ID}"
   ```

5. **Configure Route Tables for App Tier and DB Tier**:
   ```bash
   # App Route Table (points 0.0.0.0/0 to NAT Gateway)
   APP_RT=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --region "${REGION}" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=route-table,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=app-tier-rt}]' --query "RouteTable.RouteTableId" --output text)
   aws ec2 create-route --region "${REGION}" --route-table-id "${APP_RT}" --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --nat-gateway-id "${NAT_GW_ID}"
   aws ec2 associate-route-table --region "${REGION}" --subnet-id "${APP_SUB_A}" --route-table-id "${APP_RT}"
   aws ec2 associate-route-table --region "${REGION}" --subnet-id "${APP_SUB_B}" --route-table-id "${APP_RT}"

   # DB Route Table (isolated, local routing only - no 0.0.0.0/0 route)
   DB_RT=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --region "${REGION}" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=route-table,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=db-tier-isolated-rt}]' --query "RouteTable.RouteTableId" --output text)
   aws ec2 associate-route-table --region "${REGION}" --subnet-id "${DB_SUB_A}" --route-table-id "${DB_RT}"
   aws ec2 associate-route-table --region "${REGION}" --subnet-id "${DB_SUB_B}" --route-table-id "${DB_RT}"
   ```

6. **Create Three-Tier Chained Security Groups**:
   ```bash
   # 1. Public Load Balancer Security Group
   ALB_SG=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --region "${REGION}" --group-name "public-alb-sg" --description "Public internet facing ALB" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --query "GroupId" --output text)
   aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --region "${REGION}" --group-id "${ALB_SG}" --protocol tcp --port 80 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
   aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --region "${REGION}" --group-id "${ALB_SG}" --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

   # 2. App Tier Security Group (only accepts traffic from ALB SG)
   APP_SG=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --region "${REGION}" --group-name "app-tier-sg" --description "Private app servers" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --query "GroupId" --output text)
   aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --region "${REGION}" --group-id "${APP_SG}" --protocol tcp --port 8080 --source-group "${ALB_SG}"

   # 3. Database Tier Security Group (only accepts traffic from App SG)
   DB_SG=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --region "${REGION}" --group-name "db-tier-sg" --description "Private database instances" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --query "GroupId" --output text)
   aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --region "${REGION}" --group-id "${DB_SG}" --protocol tcp --port 5432 --source-group "${APP_SG}"

   echo "ALB SG: ${ALB_SG} -> App SG: ${APP_SG} -> DB SG: ${DB_SG}"
   ```

7. **Verify Architecture Configuration**:
   ```bash
   aws ec2 describe-subnets --region "${REGION}" --filters "Name=vpc-id,Values=${VPC_ID}" --query "Subnets[*].[Tags[?Key=='Name'].Value|[0],CidrBlock,AvailabilityZone]" --output table
   aws ec2 describe-route-tables --region "${REGION}" --filters "Name=vpc-id,Values=${VPC_ID}" --query "RouteTables[*].[Tags[?Key=='Name'].Value|[0],Routes[*].GatewayId]" --output json
   ```

## Done When
- [ ] 6 subnets created across two Availability Zones (`us-east-1a` and `us-east-1b`).
- [ ] Internet Gateway attached to VPC and linked to public subnets via `public-rt`.
- [ ] NAT Gateway provisioned in a public subnet with an allocated Elastic IP.
- [ ] App subnets associated with `app-tier-rt` pointing `0.0.0.0/0` to the NAT Gateway.
- [ ] DB subnets associated with `db-tier-isolated-rt` containing only local VPC routing.
- [ ] Security group chaining verified: Internet -> `ALB_SG` -> `APP_SG` -> `DB_SG`.

## Cost and Cleanup
> [!IMPORTANT]
> **NAT Gateways incur an hourly charge** (~$0.045 per hour + data processing). Unattached Elastic IPs also incur ~$0.005/hour. To maintain a **$0.00 to <$0.02** lab cost, execute the teardown commands below immediately upon completing your verification.

Execute full teardown in strict dependency order:
```bash
REGION="us-east-1"

echo "Beginning Three-Tier VPC Teardown..."

# 1. Delete NAT Gateway and release Elastic IP
aws ec2 delete-nat-gateway --region "${REGION}" --nat-gateway-id "${NAT_GW_ID}"
echo "Waiting for NAT Gateway to delete (takes ~2 minutes)..."
aws ec2 wait nat-gateway-deleted --region "${REGION}" --nat-gateway-ids "${NAT_GW_ID}"

aws ec2 release-address --region "${REGION}" --allocation-id "${EIP_ALLOC_ID}"
echo "Released Elastic IP: ${EIP_ALLOC_ID}"

# 2. Delete Security Groups (DB SG -> App SG -> ALB SG)
aws ec2 delete-security-group --region "${REGION}" --group-id "${DB_SG}"
aws ec2 delete-security-group --region "${REGION}" --group-id "${APP_SG}"
aws ec2 delete-security-group --region "${REGION}" --group-id "${ALB_SG}"

# 3. Disassociate and delete custom route tables
for RT in "${PUB_RT}" "${APP_RT}" "${DB_RT}"; do
  for ASSOC in $(aws ec2 describe-route-tables --region "${REGION}" --route-table-ids "${RT}" --query "RouteTables[0].Associations[*].RouteTableAssociationId" --output text); do
    [ "${ASSOC}" != "None" ] && aws ec2 disassociate-route-table --region "${REGION}" --association-id "${ASSOC}"
  done
  aws ec2 delete-route-table --region "${REGION}" --route-table-id "${RT}"
done

# 4. Detach and delete Internet Gateway
aws ec2 detach-internet-gateway --region "${REGION}" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}" --internet-gateway-id "${IGW_ID}"
aws ec2 delete-internet-gateway --region "${REGION}" --internet-gateway-id "${IGW_ID}"

# 5. Delete all 6 subnets
for SUB in "${PUB_SUB_A}" "${PUB_SUB_B}" "${APP_SUB_A}" "${APP_SUB_B}" "${DB_SUB_A}" "${DB_SUB_B}"; do
  aws ec2 delete-subnet --region "${REGION}" --subnet-id "${SUB}"
done

# 6. Delete VPC
aws ec2 delete-vpc --region "${REGION}" --vpc-id "${VPC_ID}"

echo "Three-tier VPC architecture destroyed successfully."
```

## Azure / GCP Equivalents
| Architecture Layer | AWS | Azure Equivalent | GCP Equivalent |
|--------------------|-----|------------------|----------------|
| Ingress / Public Tier | Public Subnet + Internet Gateway + ALB | Frontend Subnet + Public IP + Azure Application Gateway | Public Subnet + Cloud Load Balancing |
| Egress Gateway | NAT Gateway + Elastic IP | Azure NAT Gateway | Cloud NAT Gateway |
| Application Tier | Private Subnet + EC2 App Instances | App Subnet + Virtual Machine Scale Set (VMSS) | Private Subnet + Managed Instance Group (MIG) |
| Database Tier | Isolated Private Subnet + RDS Multi-AZ | Database Subnet + Azure Database with VNet Injection | Private Service Connect / Private DB Subnet + Cloud SQL |
| Tier Firewall Isolation | Chained Security Groups | Network Security Groups (NSGs) with ASGs | VPC Firewall Rules with Service Account tags |

- 📖 [Azure Three-Tier Architecture Guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/reference-architectures/n-tier/n-tier-iaas)
- 📖 [Google Cloud Three-Tier Architecture](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/three-tier-web-app)

## Stretch Goal
Automate the entire three-tier architecture deployment: Convert this AWS CLI script into an infrastructure-as-code template using AWS CloudFormation or HashiCorp Terraform. Parameterize the VPC CIDR block and Availability Zones so the entire topology can be launched and destroyed with a single command.

## Common Mistakes
- **Placing the NAT Gateway in a private subnet**: A NAT Gateway must be placed in a **public subnet** with an attached Elastic IP and a route to the Internet Gateway; otherwise, it cannot route outbound traffic to the internet.
- **Forgetting to release the Elastic IP after deleting the NAT Gateway**: An unassociated Elastic IP sitting idle in your AWS account incurs continuous hourly billing ($0.005/hr). Always run `aws ec2 release-address`.
- **Accidentally attaching the default route to the database route table**: The database tier must be strictly isolated. Giving database subnets a route to an IGW or NAT Gateway violates defense-in-depth principles.

# Day 41: What Are Containers?
[← Previous Day](../day-40-three-tier-vpc/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-42-docker-basics/README.md)

## Goal
Understand the core concepts of containers, how they fundamentally differ from virtual machines, and the Linux kernel primitives (namespaces and cgroups) that make container isolation possible.

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 60 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [Docker Overview — Architecture and Concepts](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-overview/) — Official guide explaining the Docker engine architecture, images, containers, and registries.
- 📖 [Docker Get Started Guide](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/) — High-level walkthrough of containerization fundamentals and terminology.

## Do
In this exercise, you will explore the exact Linux operating system features that enable containerization: Namespaces (isolation) and Control Groups (resource limits).

1. Open your terminal (Linux host, VM, or WSL2 on Windows).

2. Inspect the Linux process tree on your system to see how standard processes share a single kernel:
   ```bash
   ps -ef | head -n 20
   ```

3. View the active Linux namespaces currently registered by your operating system:
   ```bash
   lsns
   ```
   Notice the namespace types listed: `net` (networking), `pid` (process IDs), `mnt` (mount points), `ipc` (inter-process communication), `uts` (hostname), and `user` (user mapping). Containers use these exact namespaces to create an isolated runtime box.

4. Inspect the Control Groups (cgroups) supported by your running kernel:
   ```bash
   cat /proc/cgroups
   ```
   Look at controllers such as `cpu`, `memory`, `pids`, and `blkio`. When Docker restricts a container to "512 MB RAM", it configures the `memory` cgroup.

5. Test process isolation manually using the standard Linux `unshare` tool to see how a new hostname namespace works:
   ```bash
   # Run a subshell with an isolated UTS (hostname) namespace
   sudo unshare --uts bash
   
   # Change the hostname in this isolated shell
   hostname container-test
   
   # Verify the new hostname inside this namespace
   hostname
   
   # Exit the subshell
   exit
   
   # Verify that your host machine's hostname remains untouched
   hostname
   ```

6. Summarize the VM vs. Container comparison in your notes:
   - **Virtual Machines:** Include a full guest OS, virtual BIOS, virtual virtualized hardware, managed by a Hypervisor (Type 1 or Type 2). Heavyweight (GBs, minutes to boot).
   - **Containers:** Share the host OS kernel, package only the application binaries and dependencies, isolated via namespaces and cgroups. Lightweight (MBs, milliseconds to boot).

## Done When
- [ ] You can explain why containers start in sub-seconds compared to virtual machines.
- [ ] You verified your host's active namespaces using `lsns`.
- [ ] You inspected `/proc/cgroups` to see resource controllers.
- [ ] You successfully tested isolated namespaces using the `unshare` command without modifying your host system.

## Cost and Cleanup
$0 — no cloud resources used (run locally on your Linux machine or WSL2). No background processes were left running, so no cleanup is required.

## Stretch Goal
Explore how container filesystems work by examining the `chroot` command (`man chroot`). Read about the Open Container Initiative (OCI) image and runtime specifications to understand how industry standards ensure container portability across different container engines (Docker, Podman, containerd).

## Common Mistakes
- **Confusing containers with miniature virtual machines:** Containers do not boot an independent operating system kernel. They are simply isolated standard processes running directly on the host's Linux kernel.
- **Assuming container security equals VM isolation:** Because containers share the host kernel, a vulnerability in the host kernel can affect all containers on that host if containers are run with root privileges. Always follow the principle of least privilege.
- **Trying to run native Linux containers on bare Windows/macOS without a VM:** Linux containers require a Linux kernel. On macOS and Windows, Docker uses a lightweight Linux VM (such as WSL2 on Windows or HyperKit/Virtualization framework on macOS) behind the scenes to provide the Linux kernel.

# Day 42: Docker Installation and Basics
[← Previous Day](../day-41-what-are-containers/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-43-dockerfiles/README.md)

## Goal
Install the Docker Engine and master essential Docker CLI commands to run, inspect, manage, and remove containerized applications.

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 75 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [Docker Engine Installation Guides](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/) — Official documentation detailing installation steps across Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, macOS, and Windows.
- 📖 [Docker CLI Container Run Reference](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/) — Official reference for `docker run`, flags (`-d`, `-it`, `-p`, `--name`), and process execution.

## Do
1. Verify or install Docker on your machine.
   - For Ubuntu / Debian / WSL2:
     ```bash
     # Check if Docker is already installed
     docker --version
     ```
     If Docker is not installed, install the Docker Engine following the [official Ubuntu guide](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/ubuntu/):
     ```bash
     sudo apt-get update
     sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl gnupg
     sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
     curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg
     sudo chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg

     echo \
       "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu \
       $(. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_CODENAME") stable" | \
       sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null

     sudo apt-get update
     sudo apt-get install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin
     ```

2. Test your Docker installation with the standard hello-world container:
   ```bash
   sudo docker run hello-world
   ```
   Observe the output: Docker looks for the image locally, doesn't find it, downloads it from Docker Hub, and runs it inside a new container.

3. Run an interactive container using an official Ubuntu image:
   ```bash
   sudo docker run -it --name my-ubuntu ubuntu:22.04 bash
   ```
   You are now inside the container shell! Test a few commands inside the container:
   ```bash
   cat /etc/os-release
   whoami
   exit
   ```

4. Run a background (detached) web server using Nginx with port forwarding:
   ```bash
   sudo docker run -d --name my-web -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine
   ```

5. Verify that the web server is running and accessible:
   ```bash
   curl http://localhost:8080
   ```
   You should see the default "Welcome to nginx!" HTML response.

6. Inspect active and stopped containers:
   ```bash
   # List currently running containers
   sudo docker ps

   # List all containers (including exited ones)
   sudo docker ps -a

   # Check logs of the running web container
   sudo docker logs my-web

   # Check resource usage (CPU/Memory)
   sudo docker stats --no-stream
   ```

7. Stop and clean up the test containers:
   ```bash
   sudo docker stop my-web
   sudo docker rm my-web my-ubuntu
   ```

## Done When
- [ ] `docker --version` reports a modern Docker version.
- [ ] You successfully ran `docker run hello-world` and inspected the download process.
- [ ] You interacted with a container shell using `docker run -it`.
- [ ] You ran a detached web container (`-d`), mapped port `8080:80`, and verified the response via `curl`.
- [ ] You practiced container lifecycle commands: `docker ps`, `docker logs`, `docker stop`, and `docker rm`.

## Cost and Cleanup
$0 — no cloud resources used (runs 100% locally).

Clean up local images and containers created during this lab:
```bash
sudo docker stop my-web 2>/dev/null || true
sudo docker rm my-web my-ubuntu 2>/dev/null || true
sudo docker rmi hello-world nginx:alpine ubuntu:22.04 2>/dev/null || true
```

## Stretch Goal
Avoid typing `sudo` for every Docker command by adding your Linux user account to the `docker` group:
```bash
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
```
Log out and log back in (or run `newgrp docker`) to apply the change, then verify running `docker ps` without `sudo`. Research the security implication: members of the `docker` group have privileges equivalent to root on the host system because the Docker daemon runs with root privileges.

## Common Mistakes
- **Permission denied connecting to docker.sock:** If running `docker ps` throws `permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket`, either prepend commands with `sudo` or add your user to the `docker` group and re-authenticate.
- **Port mapping confusion (`-p HOST:CONTAINER`):** A common mistake is flipping the ports. The syntax is always `host_port:container_port`. For example, `-p 8080:80` maps host port 8080 to container port 80.
- **Thinking `docker stop` deletes the container:** Stopping a container only halts its execution. The container files and configuration still exist on disk. Use `docker rm <container-id>` to permanently delete the container, or use `docker run --rm` to auto-remove when it exits.

# Day 43: Dockerfiles and Building Images
[← Previous Day](../day-42-docker-basics/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-44-docker-networking-volumes/README.md)

## Goal
Write an optimized Dockerfile, understand how layer caching accelerates builds, package a custom Python Flask application into an image, and run it locally.

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 90 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [Dockerfile Reference](https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/) — Official specification for all Dockerfile instructions including `FROM`, `WORKDIR`, `COPY`, `RUN`, `ENV`, `EXPOSE`, and `CMD`.
- 📖 [Dockerfile Best Practices](https://docs.docker.com/develop/develop-images/dockerfile_best-practices/) — Official best practices covering image layer minimization, build cache optimization, and security hygiene.

## Do
In this lab, you will use the sample application and Dockerfile located in the repository under [`labs/docker/`](../../labs/docker/).

1. Navigate to the Docker lab folder in your terminal:
   ```bash
   cd "labs/docker"
   ```

2. Inspect the application files:
   - Examine [`app.py`](../../labs/docker/app.py) — a simple Flask web service that provides a greeting and a `/health` endpoint.
   - Examine [`requirements.txt`](../../labs/docker/requirements.txt) — declares dependencies (`flask`, `redis`).
   - Examine [`Dockerfile`](../../labs/docker/Dockerfile):
     ```dockerfile
     # Use an official lightweight Python image
     FROM python:3.11-slim

     # Set working directory inside container
     WORKDIR /app

     # Set environment variables to prevent Python from writing pyc files and buffering stdout/stderr
     ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
         PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

     # Copy requirements file first for layer caching
     COPY requirements.txt .

     # Install dependencies
     RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

     # Copy application source code
     COPY app.py .

     # Expose port 5000 for web traffic
     EXPOSE 5000

     # Run Flask application using python
     CMD ["python", "app.py"]
     ```

3. Notice the layer caching design:
   - `COPY requirements.txt .` and `RUN pip install ...` come **before** `COPY app.py .`.
   - When you edit your application code in `app.py`, Docker will reuse the cached dependency layer and skip re-downloading packages, saving substantial build time!

4. Build your custom Docker image with the tag `cloud-flask-app:1.0`:
   ```bash
   docker build -t cloud-flask-app:1.0 .
   ```
   *(Note the period `.` at the end, which sets the current directory as the build context).*

5. Inspect your newly created image and its constituent layers:
   ```bash
   # List images to verify size and image ID
   docker images | grep cloud-flask-app

   # Inspect each layer instruction and its size contribution
   docker history cloud-flask-app:1.0
   ```

6. Run a container from your custom image in detached mode:
   ```bash
   docker run -d --name my-flask-app -p 5000:5000 cloud-flask-app:1.0
   ```

7. Test your running container endpoints:
   ```bash
   # Check the main greeting endpoint
   curl http://localhost:5000/

   # Check the health check endpoint
   curl http://localhost:5000/health
   ```

8. Test layer caching in practice:
   - Add a comment or print statement to `app.py`.
   - Rebuild the image with tag `cloud-flask-app:1.1`:
     ```bash
     docker build -t cloud-flask-app:1.1 .
     ```
   - Notice how steps 1 through 5 output `CACHED` and finish in under 1 second.

## Done When
- [ ] You reviewed and can explain every instruction in [`labs/docker/Dockerfile`](../../labs/docker/Dockerfile).
- [ ] You built the image using `docker build -t cloud-flask-app:1.0 .`.
- [ ] You inspected image layers using `docker history`.
- [ ] You ran the container and received HTTP 200 JSON responses on port 5000.
- [ ] You experienced Docker layer caching when rebuilding the image.

## Cost and Cleanup
$0 — no cloud resources used (runs locally).

To tear down the running container and clean up the test images:
```bash
docker stop my-flask-app 2>/dev/null || true
docker rm my-flask-app 2>/dev/null || true
docker rmi cloud-flask-app:1.0 cloud-flask-app:1.1 2>/dev/null || true
```

## Stretch Goal
Create a `.dockerignore` file in `labs/docker/` with the following contents:
```
__pycache__/
*.pyc
*.pyo
*.pyd
.git
.env
.pytest_cache/
```
Verify that excluded files are no longer sent to the Docker daemon build context. Read about multi-stage builds in the Docker documentation to see how compiled languages separate the build environment from the minimal runtime image.

## Common Mistakes
- **Forgetting the build context dot (`.`):** Running `docker build -t my-app` without the final dot will result in a syntax error because Docker requires the path to the build context.
- **Copying source code before installing dependencies:** Placing `COPY . .` before `RUN pip install` causes Docker to invalidate the cache and reinstall all packages whenever any file in the directory changes.
- **Using heavy base images:** Using `FROM python:3.11` (full Debian, ~1GB) instead of `FROM python:3.11-slim` or `alpine` produces bloated images that take longer to build, pull, and scan.

# Day 44: Docker Networking and Volumes
[← Previous Day](../day-43-dockerfiles/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-45-docker-compose/README.md)

## Goal
Master Docker networking to enable secure inter-container communication using built-in DNS, and configure Docker volumes and bind mounts for robust data persistence.

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 90 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [Docker Networking Overview](https://docs.docker.com/network/) — Official documentation on Docker network drivers (bridge, host, overlay), network isolation, and user-defined bridge networks.
- 📖 [Docker Storage and Volumes Guide](https://docs.docker.com/storage/) — Official guide detailing the key differences between named volumes, bind mounts, and temporary storage (tmpfs).

## Do
### Part 1: Docker Networking and DNS Resolution

1. View the default networks created by the Docker daemon:
   ```bash
   docker network ls
   ```
   You will see three default networks: `bridge`, `host`, and `none`.

2. Create a user-defined bridge network named `app-net`:
   ```bash
   docker network create app-net
   ```
   > **Why custom bridge networks matter:** Containers attached to user-defined bridge networks automatically resolve each other by container name via Docker's embedded DNS server. The default `bridge` network does NOT support automatic name resolution!

3. Launch a Redis container attached to `app-net`:
   ```bash
   docker run -d --name redis-server --network app-net redis:7-alpine
   ```

4. Verify DNS resolution from another container on the same network:
   ```bash
   docker run --rm --network app-net alpine ping -c 3 redis-server
   ```
   Notice that `redis-server` resolves directly to the internal IP address assigned by Docker!

5. Connect the Flask web application from Day 43 to the same network:
   ```bash
   docker run -d \
     --name flask-app \
     --network app-net \
     -e REDIS_HOST=redis-server \
     -p 5000:5000 \
     cloud-flask-app:1.0
   ```

6. Send requests to the web app:
   ```bash
   curl http://localhost:5000/
   curl http://localhost:5000/
   ```
   Notice that `redis_connected` is now `true`, and the `visits` counter increments with every request.

---

### Part 2: Persistent Storage with Docker Volumes

7. Inspect container ephemeral behavior: By default, any data written inside a container lives in the writable container layer and is permanently lost when the container is deleted. To persist data, we use **Docker Volumes**.

8. Create a named volume for database persistence:
   ```bash
   docker volume create db-data
   docker volume ls
   docker volume inspect db-data
   ```

9. Launch a Redis container using the volume:
   ```bash
   docker run -d --name persistent-redis -v db-data:/data redis:7-alpine
   ```

10. Store a key-value pair in Redis and force an immediate save to disk:
    ```bash
    docker exec persistent-redis redis-cli set engineer "Cloud Hero"
    docker exec persistent-redis redis-cli save
    docker exec persistent-redis redis-cli get engineer
    ```

11. Simulate a container failure by forcefully stopping and deleting the container:
    ```bash
    docker rm -f persistent-redis
    ```

12. Start a brand-new container attached to the existing `db-data` volume:
    ```bash
    docker run -d --name new-redis -v db-data:/data redis:7-alpine
    ```

13. Retrieve the key from the new container:
    ```bash
    docker exec new-redis redis-cli get engineer
    ```
    The value `"Cloud Hero"` is retrieved! Your data survived the container destruction.

14. Test a host **Bind Mount** (commonly used in development environments for live code reloading):
    ```bash
    # Mount the current directory into an alpine container's /workspace
    docker run --rm -v "$(pwd):/workspace" -w /workspace alpine ls -la
    ```

## Done When
- [ ] You created a custom bridge network and verified container name resolution with `ping`.
- [ ] You connected two separate containers (`flask-app` and `redis-server`) across a shared custom network.
- [ ] You created a named Docker volume (`db-data`) and mounted it to a container.
- [ ] You verified data persistence by deleting a container and recovering its state in a replacement container.
- [ ] You can describe the differences between named volumes and host bind mounts.

## Cost and Cleanup
$0 — all resources run locally on your system.

Clean up the lab containers, network, and volume:
```bash
docker rm -f flask-app redis-server new-redis 2>/dev/null || true
docker network rm app-net 2>/dev/null || true
docker volume rm db-data 2>/dev/null || true
```

## Stretch Goal
Inspect a running container's network namespace and settings using `docker inspect flask-app --format '{{json .NetworkSettings.Networks}}' | jq`. Research the `host` network driver (`--network host`) to understand how high-performance services bypass the Docker virtual bridge.

## Common Mistakes
- **Assuming the default `bridge` provides DNS lookup:** Containers on the default `bridge` network cannot resolve each other by container name (e.g. `ping redis-server` fails). Always create a user-defined network (`docker network create`) for multi-container communication.
- **Forgetting that container storage is ephemeral:** Writing database files or stateful uploads directly into the container filesystem without a volume means data will be destroyed when the container is recreated or upgraded.
- **Using relative paths for bind mounts:** Bind mounts require absolute paths (e.g., `-v "$(pwd)/data:/data"` instead of `-v "./data:/data"`).

# Day 45: Docker Compose
[← Previous Day](../day-44-docker-networking-volumes/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-46-container-registries/README.md)

## Goal
Declaratively define, configure, and orchestrate a multi-container application stack (web application + database) using Docker Compose.

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 90 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [Docker Compose Overview](https://docs.docker.com/compose/) — Official documentation explaining multi-container orchestration, Compose commands, and project lifecycles.
- 📖 [Docker Compose File Reference](https://docs.docker.com/compose/compose-file/) — Official reference covering `services`, `build`, `ports`, `environment`, `depends_on`, and `volumes`.

## Do
Rather than typing lengthy `docker run` commands with dozens of flags for every container, network, and volume, **Docker Compose** lets you define your entire application architecture in a single declarative YAML configuration.

1. Verify that the Docker Compose CLI plugin is installed:
   ```bash
   docker compose version
   ```
   *(Note: Modern Docker uses `docker compose` with a space, which replaces the legacy standalone `docker-compose` v1 tool).*

2. Navigate to the lab directory:
   ```bash
   cd "labs/docker"
   ```

3. Review the declarative configuration in [`docker-compose.yml`](../../labs/docker/docker-compose.yml):
   ```yaml
   services:
     web:
       build: .
       container_name: cloud-web-app
       ports:
         - "5000:5000"
       environment:
         - REDIS_HOST=redis
         - REDIS_PORT=6379
       depends_on:
         - redis
       restart: unless-stopped

     redis:
       image: redis:7-alpine
       container_name: cloud-redis
       ports:
         - "6379:6379"
       volumes:
         - redis_data:/data
       restart: unless-stopped

   volumes:
     redis_data:
   ```

4. Key concepts to note in this file:
   - **Automatic Networking:** Docker Compose automatically creates a shared default network for all services in the file. The `web` service can communicate with Redis using the hostname `redis`.
   - **`build: .`**: Directs Compose to build the local Dockerfile before launching the service.
   - **`depends_on`**: Dictates container startup order (`redis` starts before `web`).
   - **`volumes`**: Declaratively defines persistent storage (`redis_data`) mounted to `/data`.

5. Launch the entire application stack in detached mode:
   ```bash
   docker compose up -d --build
   ```
   Notice how Docker builds the image, creates the network, creates the volume, and starts both containers simultaneously.

6. Inspect running services and their health status:
   ```bash
   docker compose ps
   ```

7. Stream unified, color-coded logs across all containers in the stack:
   ```bash
   docker compose logs -f --tail=20
   ```
   *(Press `Ctrl+C` to stop streaming logs).*

8. Test the running multi-tier application:
   ```bash
   curl http://localhost:5000/
   curl http://localhost:5000/
   curl http://localhost:5000/
   ```
   Each request increments the visitor counter stored inside Redis!

9. Run an ad-hoc command inside one of the managed containers:
   ```bash
   docker compose exec redis redis-cli get visits
   ```

10. Practice Compose lifecycle commands:
    ```bash
    # Temporarily pause containers
    docker compose stop

    # Resume containers
    docker compose start

    # View process list in the stack
    docker compose top
    ```

11. Tear down the stack:
    ```bash
    docker compose down
    ```
    To also delete the persistent volume, run:
    ```bash
    docker compose down -v
    ```

## Done When
- [ ] You confirmed Docker Compose plugin is working (`docker compose version`).
- [ ] You reviewed each section of [`labs/docker/docker-compose.yml`](../../labs/docker/docker-compose.yml).
- [ ] You started the entire two-tier stack with `docker compose up -d`.
- [ ] You verified container status with `docker compose ps` and logs with `docker compose logs`.
- [ ] You verified that `web` successfully communicated with `redis` over the automatic Compose network.
- [ ] You gracefully stopped and tore down the stack using `docker compose down -v`.

## Cost and Cleanup
$0 — no cloud resources used (runs completely on your local workstation).

To ensure all containers, networks, and lab volumes are completely cleaned up:
```bash
cd "labs/docker"
docker compose down -v 2>/dev/null || true
```

## Stretch Goal
Create a `.env` file in `labs/docker/` with the following variables:
```
WEB_PORT=8000
REDIS_VERSION=7-alpine
```
Update [`docker-compose.yml`](../../labs/docker/docker-compose.yml) to use `${WEB_PORT}:5000` and `image: redis:${REDIS_VERSION}`. Relaunch with `docker compose up -d` to see how environment variables make Compose configurations dynamic across development and production environments.

## Common Mistakes
- **Assuming `depends_on` waits for application readiness:** `depends_on` only waits until the container has started, not until the application inside (like Redis or PostgreSQL) is ready to accept socket connections. For production systems, combine `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy` and a container `healthcheck`.
- **Typing legacy `docker-compose` instead of `docker compose`:** The hyphenated command `docker-compose` is v1 (deprecated Python binary). Always use the modern `docker compose` CLI plugin.
- **Forgetting that `docker compose down` preserves volumes:** Running `docker compose down` stops containers and removes networks, but preserves named volumes to prevent accidental data loss. Add the `-v` flag (`docker compose down -v`) if you explicitly want a completely fresh database state.

# Day 46: Container Registries (ECR, Docker Hub)
[← Previous Day](../day-45-docker-compose/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-47-multi-stage-builds/README.md)

## Goal
Build, tag, and publish container images to public and private container registries including Docker Hub and Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR).

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 90 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [Docker Hub Quickstart](https://docs.docker.com/docker-hub/) — Official Docker guide explaining image repositories, tags, authentication, and push/pull workflows.
- 📖 [Amazon ECR User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/) — Official AWS guide covering private ECR repositories, authentication tokens, and lifecycle policies.

## Do
A container image built on your laptop only exists locally. To deploy it to servers, cloud virtual machines, or Kubernetes clusters, you store it in a centralized **container registry**.

### Part 1: Tagging and Docker Hub

1. Check your existing local image from the Day 43 lab or build one now:
   ```bash
   cd "labs/docker"
   docker build -t cloud-app:v1.0.0 .
   ```

2. Understand the Docker image tagging convention:
   ```
   [registry-host/][namespace/]repository-name:tag
   ```
   When no registry host is specified, Docker defaults to Docker Hub (`docker.io`).

3. Tag the image with your Docker Hub username (replace `YOUR_DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` with your handle, or test with a local dummy tag):
   ```bash
   export DOCKER_USER="YOUR_DOCKERHUB_USERNAME"
   docker tag cloud-app:v1.0.0 "${DOCKER_USER}/cloud-app:1.0.0"
   docker tag cloud-app:v1.0.0 "${DOCKER_USER}/cloud-app:latest"
   ```

4. View your tagged images:
   ```bash
   docker images | grep cloud-app
   ```
   Notice that both tags share the exact same `IMAGE ID`—tags are simply pointers (aliases) to immutable image digests.

5. (Optional, if you have a Docker Hub account) Authenticate and push:
   ```bash
   docker login -u "${DOCKER_USER}"
   docker push "${DOCKER_USER}/cloud-app:1.0.0"
   docker push "${DOCKER_USER}/cloud-app:latest"
   ```

### Part 2: Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR)

6. Set your target AWS region and create a private ECR repository:
   ```bash
   export AWS_REGION="us-east-1"
   export REPO_NAME="cloud-engineering-app"

   aws ecr create-repository \
     --repository-name "${REPO_NAME}" \
     --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true \
     --region "${AWS_REGION}"
   ```

7. Retrieve your AWS Account ID and construct your ECR registry URI:
   ```bash
   ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
   ECR_REGISTRY="${ACCOUNT_ID}.dkr.ecr.${AWS_REGION}.amazonaws.com"
   ECR_REPO_URI="${ECR_REGISTRY}/${REPO_NAME}"
   echo "ECR Repository URI: ${ECR_REPO_URI}"
   ```

8. Authenticate your local Docker client to the private ECR registry:
   ```bash
   aws ecr get-login-password --region "${AWS_REGION}" | \
     docker login --username AWS --password-stdin "${ECR_REGISTRY}"
   ```
   *(The `aws ecr get-login-password` command generates a short-lived 12-hour authentication token that Docker uses as its password).*

9. Tag your local image for Amazon ECR:
   ```bash
   docker tag cloud-app:v1.0.0 "${ECR_REPO_URI}:1.0.0"
   docker tag cloud-app:v1.0.0 "${ECR_REPO_URI}:latest"
   ```

10. Push the image to Amazon ECR:
    ```bash
    docker push "${ECR_REPO_URI}:1.0.0"
    docker push "${ECR_REPO_URI}:latest"
    ```

11. Verify the uploaded image in ECR:
    ```bash
    aws ecr describe-images \
      --repository-name "${REPO_NAME}" \
      --region "${AWS_REGION}" \
      --query "imageDetails[*].[imageTags,imagePushedAt,imageSizeInBytes]" \
      --output table
    ```

12. Test pulling the image by digest or tag from ECR:
    ```bash
    # Remove local tag first
    docker rmi "${ECR_REPO_URI}:1.0.0"

    # Pull cleanly from ECR
    docker pull "${ECR_REPO_URI}:1.0.0"
    ```

## Done When
- [ ] You understood the anatomy of a container image URI and tag.
- [ ] You tagged a local image with both semantic version (`1.0.0`) and `latest`.
- [ ] You created a private Amazon ECR repository using the AWS CLI.
- [ ] You authenticated Docker against ECR using `aws ecr get-login-password`.
- [ ] You pushed your image to ECR and verified its presence with `aws ecr describe-images`.
- [ ] You cleaned up the cloud repository to prevent storage charges.

## Cost and Cleanup
Expected Cost: **$0.00** — ECR offers 500 MB/month of storage in the AWS Free Tier. However, repositories should be deleted to prevent ongoing storage charges.

Delete the ECR repository and its images:
```bash
aws ecr delete-repository \
  --repository-name "${REPO_NAME}" \
  --region "${AWS_REGION}" \
  --force

# Remove local cloud tags
docker rmi "${ECR_REPO_URI}:latest" 2>/dev/null || true
```

## Azure / GCP Equivalents
| AWS | Azure | GCP |
|-----|-------|-----|
| Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) | Azure Container Registry (ACR) | Artifact Registry (formerly Container Registry) |
| `aws ecr get-login-password` | `az acr login --name <registry>` | `gcloud auth configure-docker` |
| ECR Public Gallery | Microsoft Artifact Registry / Docker Hub | Artifact Registry Public Repositories |

- 📖 [Azure Container Registry Documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/)
- 📖 [Google Cloud Artifact Registry Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/artifact-registry/docs)

## Stretch Goal
Configure an **ECR Lifecycle Policy** JSON file that automatically expires untagged images older than 7 days, or keeps only the last 5 tagged images. Apply it with:
```bash
aws ecr put-lifecycle-policy \
  --repository-name "${REPO_NAME}" \
  --lifecycle-policy-text '{"rules":[{"rulePriority":1,"description":"Expire untagged images","selection":{"tagStatus":"untagged","countType":"sinceImagePushed","countUnit":"days","countNumber":7},"action":{"type":"expire"}}]}' \
  --region "${AWS_REGION}"
```

## Common Mistakes
- **Using `latest` in production environments:** The `latest` tag is mutable and can overwrite previous builds unexpectedly, making rollbacks unpredictable. Always push and deploy immutable semantic tags (e.g., `v1.2.3` or git commit hashes like `git-sha-7a3b4c`).
- **Token expiration with `docker login`:** ECR authorization tokens expire after 12 hours. If your push fails later with `denied: Your authorization token has expired`, rerun the `aws ecr get-login-password` pipe.
- **Forgetting the `--force` flag during repository deletion:** `aws ecr delete-repository` will fail if the repository still contains container images. Use `--force` to delete the repository along with all stored images.

# Day 47: Multi-Stage Builds and Best Practices
[← Previous Day](../day-46-container-registries/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-48-what-is-kubernetes/README.md)

## Goal
Optimize container images for minimal size and hardened security using multi-stage builds, non-root users, and `.dockerignore` files.

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 75 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [Multi-Stage Builds Documentation](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/) — Official Docker guide demonstrating how to separate build dependencies from runtime environments.
- 📖 [Dockerfile Best Practices](https://docs.docker.com/develop/develop-images/dockerfile_best-practices/) — Official Docker recommendations for caching, image layers, security, and smaller image footprint.

## Do
Single-stage Dockerfiles often bundle compilation tools, headers, test suites, and temporary artifacts into the production image, increasing image size and expanding the security attack surface. **Multi-stage builds** solve this by using multiple `FROM` instructions in a single Dockerfile, transferring only the required runtime artifacts to the final lightweight image.

1. Navigate to the lab directory:
   ```bash
   cd "labs/docker"
   ```

2. Inspect the multi-stage build file [`Dockerfile.multistage`](../../labs/docker/Dockerfile.multistage):
   ```dockerfile
   # Stage 1: Build stage (builder)
   FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
   WORKDIR /build
   RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends gcc && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
   COPY requirements.txt .
   RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --user -r requirements.txt

   # Stage 2: Final runtime stage
   FROM python:3.11-slim AS runner
   WORKDIR /app
   RUN groupadd -r appgroup && useradd -r -g appgroup -s /sbin/nologin appuser
   COPY --from=builder /root/.local /home/appuser/.local
   COPY --chown=appuser:appgroup app.py .
   ENV PATH=/home/appuser/.local/bin:$PATH PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
   USER appuser
   EXPOSE 5000
   CMD ["python", "app.py"]
   ```

3. Create a `.dockerignore` file to prevent unnecessary files from bloating build contexts and busting layer caches:
   ```bash
   cat << 'EOF' > .dockerignore
   .git
   .gitignore
   __pycache__
   *.pyc
   *.pyo
   *.pyd
   .env
   .venv
   env/
   venv/
   *.md
   Dockerfile*
   docker-compose.yml
   EOF
   ```

4. Build both the standard single-stage image and the multi-stage image to compare them:
   ```bash
   # Build single-stage image
   docker build -f Dockerfile -t app:single-stage .

   # Build multi-stage image
   docker build -f Dockerfile.multistage -t app:multi-stage .
   ```

5. Compare image sizes, layer counts, and security attributes:
   ```bash
   docker images | grep -E "app\s+(single-stage|multi-stage)"
   ```
   Notice the multi-stage image separates build dependencies cleanly while creating an unprivileged user.

6. Inspect image history to see layer creation:
   ```bash
   docker history app:multi-stage
   ```

7. Verify that the multi-stage container runs as a non-root user:
   ```bash
   # Run the container
   docker run -d --name test-secure-app -p 5000:5000 app:multi-stage

   # Verify the user ID inside the running container
   docker exec test-secure-app whoami
   docker exec test-secure-app id
   ```
   The output confirms the process is running as `appuser` (UID > 100) instead of `root` (UID 0).

8. Test that the application functions normally:
   ```bash
   curl http://localhost:5000/
   ```

9. Clean up test container:
   ```bash
   docker rm -f test-secure-app
   ```

## Done When
- [ ] You created a `.dockerignore` file in the lab directory.
- [ ] You built the multi-stage image using [`labs/docker/Dockerfile.multistage`](../../labs/docker/Dockerfile.multistage).
- [ ] You compared image layers and sizes using `docker images` and `docker history`.
- [ ] You verified that the container executes under an unprivileged user (`appuser`).
- [ ] You tested the running container using `curl` and cleaned up the test instance.

## Cost and Cleanup
$0 — no cloud resources used (runs completely on your local workstation).

Remove the locally built comparison images:
```bash
docker rmi app:single-stage app:multi-stage 2>/dev/null || true
rm -f "labs/docker/.dockerignore"
```

## Azure / GCP Equivalents
| AWS | Azure | GCP |
|-----|-------|-----|
| AWS CodeBuild / ECR Image Scanning | Azure Container Registry (ACR) Tasks / Microsoft Defender for Containers | Cloud Build / Artifact Registry Vulnerability Scanning |
| IAM Least Privilege for Task Roles | Managed Identities for Azure Container Instances | Workload Identity for Cloud Run / GKE |

- 📖 [Azure Container Registry Build Tasks](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-tasks-overview)
- 📖 [Google Cloud Build Multi-stage Builds](https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/optimizing-builds/additional-steps-to-speed-up-builds)

## Stretch Goal
Use Docker BuildKit target caching or distroless base images:
1. Build only the `builder` stage for testing or linting using the `--target` flag:
   ```bash
   docker build --target builder -f Dockerfile.multistage -t app:builder-only .
   ```
2. Research GoogleContainerTools' `gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12`, which excludes package managers, shells, and system utilities altogether.

## Common Mistakes
- **Running containers as `root` (UID 0):** By default, Docker runs container processes as root. If an application vulnerability leads to remote code execution, an attacker has root privileges within the container namespace. Always create and switch to a non-root `USER`.
- **Forgetting `.dockerignore`:** Omitting `.dockerignore` sends `.git` directories, secrets, and virtual environment folders to the Docker daemon during build context evaluation, inflating build times and risking credential leaks.
- **Copying the entire source before installing dependencies:** Placing `COPY . .` before `RUN pip install` invalidates layer caching whenever any source file changes, forcing dependencies to reinstall on every build. Always copy dependency lists (`requirements.txt`, `package.json`) and run installations first.

# Day 48: What Is Kubernetes?
[← Previous Day](../day-47-multi-stage-builds/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-49-kubernetes-architecture/README.md)

## Goal
Understand the core purpose of container orchestration and install `kubectl` alongside a local development Kubernetes cluster using Minikube or Kind.

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 75 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [Kubernetes Documentation Overview](https://kubernetes.io/docs/home/) — Official introduction to Kubernetes, container orchestration challenges, and core platform capabilities.
- 📖 [Install and Set Up kubectl](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools/) — Official installation instructions for the Kubernetes command-line interface (`kubectl`).
- 📖 [minikube Start Guide](https://minikube.sigs.k8s.io/docs/start/) — Official getting-started documentation for running a single-node Kubernetes cluster locally.

## Do
While Docker runs individual containers on a single host, production cloud systems require managing hundreds or thousands of containers across fleets of physical or virtual machines. **Kubernetes** (often abbreviated as **K8s**) is an open-source container orchestration engine that automates container deployment, scaling, health checking, self-healing, and networking.

### Part 1: Verify or Install `kubectl`

1. Check if `kubectl` is already installed on your system:
   ```bash
   kubectl version --client --output=yaml
   ```

2. If `kubectl` is not present, install the latest stable binary on Linux:
   ```bash
   curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/$(curl -L -s https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt)/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
   chmod +x kubectl
   sudo mv kubectl /usr/local/bin/
   kubectl version --client
   ```

### Part 2: Start a Local Cluster (Minikube or Kind)

3. Verify that your Docker daemon is running (Minikube and Kind use Docker containers as cluster nodes):
   ```bash
   docker info >/dev/null && echo "Docker is running" || echo "Please start Docker first"
   ```

4. Choose either **Minikube** or **Kind** (Kubernetes in Docker). To start with Minikube:
   ```bash
   # If minikube is not installed:
   # curl -LO https://storage.googleapis.com/minikube/releases/latest/minikube-linux-amd64
   # sudo install minikube-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/minikube

   minikube start --driver=docker
   ```

   *(Alternative using Kind):*
   ```bash
   # If using kind instead of minikube:
   # curl -Lo ./kind https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/dl/v0.22.0/kind-linux-amd64 && chmod +x ./kind && sudo mv ./kind /usr/local/bin/kind
   # kind create cluster --name local-dev
   ```

5. Confirm cluster connectivity and view cluster endpoints:
   ```bash
   kubectl cluster-info
   ```

6. Inspect the cluster nodes:
   ```bash
   kubectl get nodes -o wide
   ```
   You should see one node in the `Ready` status.

### Part 3: Deploy Your First Pod

7. Run an ad-hoc container (a Pod) using the imperative command:
   ```bash
   kubectl run test-nginx --image=nginx:alpine --port=80
   ```

8. Check the status of your Pod:
   ```bash
   kubectl get pods -o wide
   ```
   Wait until the Pod status transitions from `ContainerCreating` to `Running`.

9. View the Pod's detailed events and metadata:
   ```bash
   kubectl describe pod test-nginx
   ```
   Notice the events at the bottom showing image pulling, container creation, and startup.

10. Forward traffic from your local machine to the Pod port:
    ```bash
    kubectl port-forward pod/test-nginx 8080:80 &
    PORT_FORWARD_PID=$!
    sleep 2

    # Query the running Pod
    curl -s http://localhost:8080 | grep -i "Welcome to nginx"
    ```

11. Clean up the forward process and delete the test Pod:
    ```bash
    kill $PORT_FORWARD_PID 2>/dev/null || true
    kubectl delete pod test-nginx
    ```

## Done When
- [ ] `kubectl` is installed and verified via `kubectl version --client`.
- [ ] A local Kubernetes cluster (Minikube or Kind) is running.
- [ ] `kubectl cluster-info` and `kubectl get nodes` return an active node in `Ready` status.
- [ ] You launched an Nginx Pod with `kubectl run` and inspected it using `kubectl describe pod`.
- [ ] You accessed the Pod via `kubectl port-forward` and successfully deleted the Pod.

## Cost and Cleanup
$0 — no cloud resources used (runs completely on your local workstation using Minikube or Kind).

To stop the cluster when finished:
```bash
# If using minikube:
minikube stop

# To completely delete the local cluster VM/containers:
# minikube delete
# (or if using kind: kind delete cluster --name local-dev)
```

## Stretch Goal
Enable bash shell autocompletion for `kubectl` so you can press `Tab` to complete resource types and pod names:
```bash
echo "source <(kubectl completion bash)" >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc
```
Try typing `kubectl get no` and press `Tab`—it will autocomplete to `kubectl get nodes`.

## Common Mistakes
- **Confusing Docker with Kubernetes:** Docker is a container runtime used to package and execute single containers. Kubernetes is an orchestrator that coordinates multiple hosts running Docker (or containerd) runtimes.
- **Running `kubectl` without a started cluster:** If you run `kubectl get nodes` before starting Minikube or Kind, you will see `The connection to the server localhost:8080 was refused`. Always start your local cluster first.
- **Using imperative `kubectl run` for production deployments:** `kubectl run` creates a standalone unmanaged Pod without replica guarantees or automatic healing. In production, always use declarative Deployments.

# Day 49: Kubernetes Architecture
[← Previous Day](../day-48-what-is-kubernetes/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-50-pods-replicasets-deployments/README.md)

## Goal
Explore and inspect the core architecture of a Kubernetes cluster, distinguishing between Control Plane components and Worker Node components.

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 75 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [Kubernetes Cluster Architecture](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/) — Official architecture guide detailing Control Plane and Worker Node separation.
- 📖 [Kubernetes Components Reference](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/components/) — In-depth breakdown of `kube-apiserver`, `etcd`, `kube-scheduler`, `kube-controller-manager`, `kubelet`, and `kube-proxy`.

## Do
A Kubernetes cluster consists of two distinct functional layers:
1. **Control Plane:** The cluster brain that makes global decisions (scheduling, detecting node failures, maintaining desired state).
2. **Worker Nodes:** The workhorse machines that run containerized workloads.

### Understanding the Key Components

| Component | Layer | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **kube-apiserver** | Control Plane | Front-end for the control plane. Exposes the Kubernetes HTTP REST API. All internal and external tools (`kubectl`, worker nodes) communicate solely through it. |
| **etcd** | Control Plane | Consistent, highly-available key-value store holding the entire cluster state and configuration. |
| **kube-scheduler** | Control Plane | Watches for newly created Pods with no assigned node and selects the best worker node for them based on resource requirements, taints, and affinity rules. |
| **kube-controller-manager**| Control Plane | Runs controller reconciliation processes (Node Controller, Job Controller, EndpointSlice Controller, ServiceAccount Controller). |
| **kubelet** | Worker Node | Agent running on each node ensuring that containers described in PodSpecs are running and healthy by communicating with the container runtime via CRI (Container Runtime Interface). |
| **kube-proxy** | Worker Node | Network proxy running on each node that maintains network rules (using iptables or IPVS) to allow network communication to Pods from inside or outside the cluster. |
| **CoreDNS** | Cluster Add-on | Provides internal cluster DNS resolution (translating service names like `redis` to cluster IP addresses). |

### Hands-on: Inspect Your Cluster Components

1. Ensure your local cluster (Minikube or Kind) is running:
   ```bash
   kubectl cluster-info
   ```

2. List all internal control plane and system pods running in the `kube-system` namespace:
   ```bash
   kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide
   ```
   Notice the pods: `kube-apiserver`, `etcd`, `kube-scheduler`, `kube-controller-manager`, `kube-proxy`, and `coredns`.

3. Inspect the `kube-apiserver` pod logs:
   ```bash
   APISERVER_POD=$(kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver -o jsonpath="{.items[0].metadata.name}")
   kubectl logs -n kube-system "${APISERVER_POD}" --tail=30
   ```

4. Inspect the cluster node's hardware capacity, allocatable resources, and system details:
   ```bash
   NODE_NAME=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath="{.items[0].metadata.name}")
   kubectl describe node "${NODE_NAME}"
   ```
   Scroll through the output and observe:
   - **Conditions:** `MemoryPressure`, `DiskPressure`, `PIDPressure`, `Ready`.
   - **Addresses:** InternalIP, Hostname.
   - **Capacity / Allocatable:** CPU cores, memory limits, and max pods allowed.
   - **System Info:** OS Image, Kernel Version, Container Runtime version (`containerd://...`), and Kubelet version.

5. View all supported API resource types in your cluster and their short names:
   ```bash
   kubectl api-resources
   ```
   Notice column values like `SHORTNAMES` (`po` for pods, `deploy` for deployments, `svc` for services) and `NAMESPACED` (whether the resource belongs to a namespace).

6. View recent cluster events across all namespaces to understand the control plane's reconciliation actions:
   ```bash
   kubectl get events -A --sort-by='.metadata.creationTimestamp' | tail -n 20
   ```

## Done When
- [ ] You identified the 4 main Control Plane components and 2 main Worker Node components.
- [ ] You listed all system pods running in the `kube-system` namespace.
- [ ] You inspected the node configuration, resource capacity, and container runtime using `kubectl describe node`.
- [ ] You explored supported API resources and shortnames using `kubectl api-resources`.
- [ ] You sorted and examined recent cluster events using `kubectl get events`.

## Cost and Cleanup
$0 — no cloud resources used (runs completely on your local workstation).

If you are pausing your study session, you can stop the local cluster:
```bash
minikube stop
```

## Stretch Goal
Inspect static pod manifests inside the control plane host. In standard Kubernetes installations, static pods for etcd, api-server, scheduler, and controller-manager are configured via YAML files in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`:
```bash
# If using minikube:
minikube ssh "sudo ls -la /etc/kubernetes/manifests"
minikube ssh "sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | grep 'image:'"
```

## Common Mistakes
- **Believing `kube-apiserver` runs containers directly:** The API server never executes containers. It only validates and persists pod manifests to `etcd`. The `kubelet` agent on the worker node receives the pod specification and instructs the container runtime (`containerd` or `CRI-O`) to start the container.
- **Directly modifying `etcd`:** Never attempt to write to or edit `etcd` directly. All operations must pass through the `kube-apiserver` to ensure schema validation, authentication, and authorization.
- **Confusing scheduling with reconciliation:** The `kube-scheduler` only decides *which* node a pod should be placed on. The `kube-controller-manager` is responsible for detecting drift and creating replacement pods when nodes fail or pods crash.
