# Day 90: Capstone Documentation and Presentation
[← Previous Day](../day-89-capstone-monitoring-security/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-91-aws-certification-paths/README.md)

## Goal
Polish repository documentation, write an architectural case study, produce a portfolio-ready demonstration, and execute a complete infrastructure teardown.

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 90 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [Writing Great Technical Documentation](https://www.writethedocs.org/guide/writing/beginners-guide-to-docs/) — Guide to structuring clear READMEs, quickstart instructions, and architecture diagrams.
- 📖 [AWS Well-Architected Framework](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html) — Official guidance on reviewing cloud workloads against the six pillars of architecture.

## Do
Congratulations on reaching Day 90! Today you finalize your Cloud-Native Task Manager project, create a polished portfolio README, document key engineering decisions, and safely tear down all cloud resources.

1. **Author the Comprehensive Project README**:
   In your capstone directory root, finalize `README.md` with badging, architecture diagrams, live endpoints, and reproduction steps:
   ```bash
   cd "$HOME/cloud-native-task-manager"
   cat <<'EOF' > README.md
   # Cloud-Native Task Manager

   A production-grade, three-tier cloud application built with Python Flask, PostgreSQL, Docker, Terraform, GitHub Actions, and AWS ECS Fargate.

   [![CI/CD Pipeline](https://github.com/your-username/cloud-native-task-manager/actions/workflows/pipeline.yml/badge.svg)](actions)
   [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
   [![Terraform](https://img.shields.io/badge/IaC-Terraform-623CE4.svg)](https://terraform.io)

   ## 📐 Architecture
   ```mermaid
   flowchart TD
       User["HTTP Client / Browser"] --> ALB["AWS Application Load Balancer"]
       ALB --> ECS["Amazon ECS Fargate (Task Manager API)"]
       ECS --> RDS[("Amazon RDS PostgreSQL")]
       ECS -.-> CW["CloudWatch Logs & Metrics"]
       ECS -.-> SM["AWS Secrets Manager"]
   ```

   ## 🚀 Features
   - **RESTful API**: Full CRUD task management with `/health` liveness checks.
   - **Infrastructure as Code**: Modular Terraform configurations for VPC, subnets, ECS, and security groups.
   - **Zero-Trust Security**: Containers in private subnets, non-root Docker execution, and least-privilege IAM roles.
   - **Automated CI/CD**: GitHub Actions pipeline covering linting, pytest, Trivy container security scanning, and automated ECR builds.
   - **Observability**: CloudWatch metrics, alarms, and structured JSON logging.

   ## 🛠️ Quickstart (Local Development)
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/your-username/cloud-native-task-manager.git
   cd cloud-native-task-manager
   docker compose up -d
   curl http://localhost:5000/health
   ```

   ## 📖 Documentation
   - [Architecture Deep Dive](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md)
   - [CI/CD Workflow Details](docs/CICD.md)
   - [Security & Threat Model](docs/SECURITY.md)
   - [Milestones & Progress](docs/MILESTONES.md)
   EOF
   ```

2. **Conduct a Well-Architected Self-Review**:
   Evaluate your project against the 6 pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework:
   - **Operational Excellence**: IaC via Terraform, automated GitHub Actions CI/CD, structured JSON logs.
   - **Security**: Private subnets, non-root container, secrets in Secrets Manager, Trivy vulnerability gating.
   - **Reliability**: Multi-AZ subnet distribution, ALB health checks, container restart policies.
   - **Performance Efficiency**: Multi-stage lightweight Docker image, serverless ECS Fargate scaling.
   - **Cost Optimization**: Right-sized container tasks (256 CPU / 512 MB), automated cost alerts.
   - **Sustainability**: Serverless container execution minimizing idle compute overhead.

3. **Record or Document a Demo Walkthrough**:
   Write a script or record a 3-5 minute screen recording highlighting:
   - Git repository structure and clean commit history.
   - GitHub Actions pipeline passing automated tests and Trivy scans.
   - Terraform planning and infrastructure outputs.
   - Live HTTP request testing against `/health` and `/api/v1/tasks`.

4. **Execute Complete Infrastructure Teardown**:
   Destroy all live AWS resources to prevent ongoing cloud charges:
   ```bash
   cd "$HOME/cloud-native-task-manager/terraform"
   terraform destroy -auto-approve || echo "No active Terraform state to destroy."

   # Clean up ECR repository and images
   aws ecr delete-repository --repository-name cloud-task-manager --force || true
   ```

5. **Final Commit & Milestone Sign-off**:
   Update `docs/MILESTONES.md` marking all items complete, and commit:
   ```bash
   cd "$HOME/cloud-native-task-manager"
   sed -i 's/\[ \]/\[x\]/g' docs/MILESTONES.md 2>/dev/null || true
   git add .
   git commit -m "feat: complete capstone project documentation, architecture review, and cleanup"
   ```

## Done When
- [ ] Root `README.md` is complete with architecture diagrams, badges, and quickstart instructions.
- [ ] AWS Well-Architected Framework self-review is documented.
- [ ] All live AWS infrastructure is destroyed with `terraform destroy`.
- [ ] All 7 Capstone sprint milestones in `docs/MILESTONES.md` are checked off.

## Cost and Cleanup
Expected Cost: **$0.00** after cleanup.

Teardown must be complete:
```bash
cd "$HOME/cloud-native-task-manager/terraform"
terraform destroy -auto-approve
aws ecr delete-repository --repository-name cloud-task-manager --force 2>/dev/null || true
```
Verify via `aws ec2 describe-instances` and `aws ecs list-clusters` that no resources remain active.

## Stretch Goal
Publish your project repository publicly on GitHub, add a link in your LinkedIn profile or portfolio site, and write a LinkedIn post or blog article summarizing what you learned building your capstone.

## Common Mistakes
- **Leaving orphan resources running after demoing**: Always verify that ALBs, NAT Gateways, and RDS instances are destroyed. They incur continuous charges.
- **Incomplete README files**: Hiring managers review your GitHub README first. If setup steps or architecture diagrams are missing, they cannot evaluate your skills.
- **Skipping the retrospective**: Documenting what broke and how you fixed it demonstrates maturity and problem-solving ability to interviewers.

# Day 91: AWS Certification Paths
[← Previous Day](../day-90-capstone-docs-presentation/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-92-study-strategies/README.md)

## Goal
Understand cloud certification roadmaps, select the right entry and associate-level certifications for your career trajectory, and map exam domains to your hands-on experience.

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 60 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [AWS Certification Overview](https://aws.amazon.com/certification/) — Official catalog of AWS Foundational, Associate, Professional, and Specialty credentials.
- 📖 [AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate Exam Guide](https://d1.awsstatic.com/training-and-certification/docs-sa-assoc/AWS-Certified-Solutions-Architect-Associate_Exam-Guide.pdf) — Official blueprint detailing exam content domains and score weighting.

## Do
In today's session, you will review the major cloud certification tracks, identify the high-impact credentials for cloud engineering roles, map your completed 90 days of coursework against official exam blueprints, and formulate an actionable target exam timeline.

1. **Compare Foundational vs. Associate vs. Professional Tiers**:
   - **Foundational (AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner - CLF-C02)**: Focuses on broad concepts, billing, cloud economics, and high-level service naming. Good for non-technical roles or complete beginners, but often skipped by engineering candidates.
   - **Associate Tiers (Core Engineering Focus)**:
     - **AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate (SAA-C03)**: Broad architectural patterns, resilience, high availability, VPC networking, compute, storage, databases, and cost optimization. The most recognized industry baseline.
     - **AWS Certified SysOps Administrator – Associate (SOA-C02)**: Operational monitoring, deployment automation, troubleshooting, CloudWatch, and systems administration.
     - **AWS Certified Developer – Associate (DVA-C03)**: Application development on AWS, Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, CI/CD with CodePipeline.
   - **Multi-Cloud Alternatives**:
     - **Azure**: AZ-900 (Fundamentals), AZ-104 (Azure Administrator Associate), AZ-305 (Azure Solutions Architect Expert).
     - **GCP**: Cloud Digital Leader, Associate Cloud Engineer (ACE).
     - **Specialty / Tool-Specific**: HashiCorp Certified: Terraform Associate, Linux Foundation CKA (Certified Kubernetes Administrator).

2. **Map 90 Days Experience to SAA-C03 Domains**:
   Review how the curriculum maps directly to the four core SAA-C03 domains:
   - **Domain 1: Design Secure Architectures (30%)**: Days 32 (IAM), 35 (Security Groups), 78-81 (Security, Least Privilege, Secrets, Container Scanning).
   - **Domain 2: Design Resilient Architectures (26%)**: Days 6 (Load Balancing), 33-34 (VPC & Subnets), 40 (Three-Tier VPC), 85-87 (Capstone Architecture & ECS).
   - **Domain 3: Design High-Performing Architectures (24%)**: Days 36-39 (EC2, S3, RDS), 41-47 (Docker), 48-56 (Kubernetes), 73-77 (Observability).
   - **Domain 4: Design Cost-Optimized Architectures (20%)**: Days 82 (Cost Optimization), 83 (Tagging & Budgets), 86 (IaC Sizing).

3. **Assess Skill Readiness**:
   Create a local markdown file `certification_plan.md` on your workstation:
   ```markdown
   # Cloud Certification Strategy

   ## Target Exam
   - **Primary Goal**: AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03)
   - **Secondary Tool Goal**: HashiCorp Certified Terraform Associate (003)
   - **Target Exam Date**: 4 to 6 weeks from curriculum completion

   ## Self-Assessment Audit
   - [x] VPC Networking & Subnet routing (Hands-on complete)
   - [x] IAM Roles, Policies, and Boundaries (Hands-on complete)
   - [x] Containerization & Orchestration (Hands-on complete)
   - [x] Terraform Infrastructure Automation (Hands-on complete)
   - [ ] Managed Storage tiers (S3 lifecycle transitions, EFS vs EBS nuances)
   - [ ] Serverless compute services (AWS Lambda event sources, Step Functions)
   ```

4. **Review Official Exam Logistics**:
   - Exam format: 65 questions (multiple choice / multiple response).
   - Time limit: 130 minutes.
   - Passing score: 720 / 1000.
   - Delivery: Pearson VUE testing center or online proctored exam.
   - Retake policy: 14-day mandatory waiting period if unsuccessful on first attempt.

## Done When
- [ ] Understand the differences between Foundational, Associate, and Specialty certifications.
- [ ] Read the official SAA-C03 exam guide domains.
- [ ] Create `certification_plan.md` with targeted certifications, target dates, and knowledge gap self-assessment.

## Cost and Cleanup
Expected Cost: **$0.00 — no cloud resources used.**

Study planning is free. (Note: Scheduling the SAA exam is $150 USD or $75 if using an AWS 50% discount voucher from a previous exam).

## Stretch Goal
Explore vendor-neutral certifications such as the [HashiCorp Terraform Associate](https://www.hashicorp.com/certifications/terraform-associate) or [Linux Foundation CKA](https://training.linuxfoundation.org/certification/certified-kubernetes-administrator-cka/) and determine if adding an IaC or Kubernetes credential strengthens your target role profile.

## Common Mistakes
- **Collecting certifications without building projects**: Certifications validate knowledge, but projects prove competence. A resume with 4 certificates and no GitHub portfolio raises red flags. Pair certs with code.
- **Spending months on Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02)**: If you completed these 90 days of hands-on engineering, you already have the practical knowledge to jump straight into the Solutions Architect Associate (SAA-C03).
- **Cramming exam dumps instead of understanding concepts**: Memorizing leaked questions leaves you unprepared for technical interviews and troubleshooting on the job. Focus on understanding *why* an architectural choice is right.

# Day 92: Study Strategies and Practice Exams
[← Previous Day](../day-91-aws-certification-paths/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-93-cloud-resume/README.md)

## Goal
Master active recall and spaced repetition study techniques, establish an effective practice exam review routine, and build a targeted revision plan for cloud exams.

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 60 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [AWS Certification Official Practice Question Sets](https://aws.amazon.com/certification/certified-solutions-architect-associate/) — Official 20-question sample sets directly from AWS Skill Builder.
- 📖 [The Feynman Technique and Spaced Repetition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaced_repetition) — Proven cognitive study methodologies for retaining deep technical concepts.

## Do
In today's session, you will learn how to dissect scenario-based cloud exam questions, create a tracking system for incorrect practice exam answers, and build a spaced-repetition study schedule.

1. **Understand Scenario Question Anatomy**:
   AWS Associate exam questions test architectural decision-making, typically requiring the **most cost-effective**, **most secure**, or **most resilient** solution that involves the **least operational overhead**:
   ```
   [Context / Current Architecture]
   A company runs an application on EC2 instances behind an ALB with an RDS MySQL database.

   [Pain Point / Requirement]
   During peak sales events, database read latency causes application timeouts.
   Budget constraints require minimizing costs and minimizing administrative burden.

   [Constraint Keyphrase]
   "Which solution addresses the latency with the LEAST operational overhead and lowest cost?"
   ```
   **Strategy**:
   - Identify the constraint keywords (*cost-effective*, *least operational overhead*, *highly available*, *real-time*).
   - Eliminate answers that introduce unnecessary servers to manage (e.g., self-hosting Redis on EC2 when Amazon ElastiCache or Aurora Read Replicas are options).
   - Eliminate answers that technically work but violate the specific constraint (e.g., upgrading to an expensive multi-terabyte instance when caching solves the read load).

2. **Set Up an "Incorrect Answers" Error Log**:
   Create a study spreadsheet or markdown document `exam_error_log.md`:
   ```markdown
   # Practice Exam Error Log

   | Date | Question Topic | Why I Chose My Answer | Why The Correct Answer Is Right | Core Concept / Doc Link |
   |:---:|:---|:---|:---|:---|
   | 2026-10-15 | S3 Storage Classes | Chose Glacier Instant Retrieval | Glacier Flexible Retrieval was required because retrieval time was acceptable up to 5 hours and cost had to be minimized | S3 Lifecycle Tiers |
   | 2026-10-16 | RDS Read Replicas vs Multi-AZ | Confused Read Replicas with Multi-AZ failover | Read Replicas offload read traffic; Multi-AZ is strictly synchronous standby for disaster recovery | RDS High Availability |
   ```

3. **Establish a 3-Week Practice Exam Routine**:
   Follow this structured cadence:
   - **Week 1 (Diagnostic)**: Take 1 full-length timed practice exam (e.g., 65 questions). Review every question — both those you missed and those you guessed correctly. Record every mistake in your error log.
   - **Week 2 (Targeted Weakness Remediation)**: Dedicate 3 days strictly to your lowest-scoring domains (e.g. S3 policies, Aurora Global Databases, Direct Connect). Take a 2nd practice exam; target >75%.
   - **Week 3 (Simulation & Readiness)**: Take 2 full exams in exam-like conditions (timed 130 min, no phone, quiet room). When you consistently achieve 80-85%+ on fresh question sets, you are ready to book and pass the exam.

4. **Curate High-Quality Practice Resources**:
   - **Official AWS Skill Builder**: Official sample question set and free practice exam.
   - **Tutorials Dojo (Jon Bonso)** 💳: Widely considered the gold standard for high-fidelity AWS exam question simulations with in-depth architectural explanations.
   - **Stephane Maarek / Adrian Cantrill Practice Tests** 💳: Comprehensive scenario coverage matching current exam outlines.

5. **Practice Explaining Architectural Decisions (The Feynman Technique)**:
   Pick three core AWS concepts and write a 2-paragraph explanation in plain English as if explaining them to a junior colleague or non-technical manager:
   1. The difference between an Application Load Balancer and a Network Load Balancer.
   2. When to choose AWS Lambda vs. Amazon ECS Fargate.
   3. The difference between AWS KMS Customer Managed Keys and AWS Managed Keys.

## Done When
- [ ] Understand the 4-step framework for dissecting scenario exam questions.
- [ ] Create `exam_error_log.md` to track missed practice questions.
- [ ] Complete the 3 conceptual Feynman explanations in your notes.
- [ ] Establish a 3-week study calendar leading up to exam day.

## Cost and Cleanup
Expected Cost: **$0.00 — no cloud resources used.**

Study strategies and practice log documentation do not incur cloud costs.

## Stretch Goal
Take an official 20-question practice test on AWS Skill Builder or review AWS official whitepapers (such as *Overview of Amazon Web Services* and *AWS Well-Architected Framework*), noting down 5 questions or architectures that challenged you.

## Common Mistakes
- **Taking practice exams repeatedly until you memorize answers**: Taking the same test 4 times gives a false sense of security because you memorize the answers rather than understanding the underlying concepts. Focus on variety.
- **Reviewing only the questions you got wrong**: Review the questions you guessed correctly too; if you did not know *why* the answer was right, it was luck.
- **Studying passively**: Reading documentation passively retains ~20% of information. Doing active recall, writing summaries, and building small test architectures in Terraform retains >80%.

# Day 93: Building Your Cloud Resume
[← Previous Day](../day-92-study-strategies/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-94-interview-prep/README.md)

## Goal
Transform your 90 days of practical hands-on labs and capstone project into a compelling, ATS-friendly cloud engineer resume and LinkedIn profile.

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 75 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [The Cloud Resume Challenge](https://cloudresumechallenge.dev/docs/the-challenge/aws/) — Industry-recognized open-source project framework for showcasing real-world cloud engineering skills.
- 📖 [Google's "XYZ" Resume Bullet Formula](https://www.inc.com/bill-murphy-jr/google-recruiters-say-these-5-resume-tips-including-x-y-z-formula-will-improve-your-odds-of-getting-hired-at-google-or-anywhere-else.html) — Guide on phrasing accomplishments: *Accomplished [X] as measured by [Y], by doing [Z]*.

## Do
In today's career milestone, you will rewrite your technical resume to showcase practical infrastructure engineering skills, format your capstone project with measurable metrics, optimize your GitHub profile, and structure your skills matrix.

1. **Adopt the Google "XYZ" Formula for Infrastructure**:
   Replace passive job descriptions with impact-driven engineering accomplishments:
   - ❌ *Weak*: "Configured AWS VPC and deployed Docker containers on ECS."
   - ✅ *Strong (XYZ)*: "Architected a multi-tier AWS VPC spanning 2 AZs and deployed containerized REST APIs onto ECS Fargate, reducing deployment time by 60% through automated GitHub Actions CI/CD pipelines."
   - ❌ *Weak*: "Used Terraform to manage cloud infrastructure."
   - ✅ *Strong (XYZ)*: "Automated provisioning of 15+ AWS resources using modular Terraform with remote S3 state locking and DynamoDB, eliminating manual configuration drift."

2. **Structure the Technical Skills Matrix**:
   Group your technical skills into clean, industry-standard categories:
   ```markdown
   ### Technical Skills
   - **Cloud Platforms**: Amazon Web Services (VPC, EC2, ECS Fargate, RDS PostgreSQL, S3, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch, IAM)
   - **Infrastructure as Code & Config**: Terraform, CloudFormation, Ansible basics
   - **Containers & Orchestration**: Docker, Docker Compose, Kubernetes, Helm, Amazon ECR
   - **CI/CD & Automation**: GitHub Actions, Bash Shell Scripting, Git, Trivy Security Scanner
   - **Languages & Databases**: Python (boto3, Flask, pytest), SQL, PostgreSQL
   - **Networking & Security**: TCP/IP, DNS, CIDR, Load Balancing (ALB), TLS/SSL, IAM Least Privilege
   ```

3. **Frame Your Capstone Project as Production Work**:
   Create a dedicated section on your resume for your capstone project:
   ```markdown
   ### Projects
   **Cloud-Native Task Manager (Production Multi-Tier Web Application)**
   *GitHub: github.com/your-username/cloud-native-task-manager | AWS | Terraform | Docker | CI/CD*
   - Engineered a 3-tier REST API backend using Python Flask and PostgreSQL with automated CRUD and health check endpoints.
   - Provisioned 100% of AWS infrastructure (custom VPC, public/private subnets across 2 AZs, security groups, ECS Fargate, RDS) using modular Terraform code.
   - Built a multi-stage Docker container image running as a non-root user, decreasing image size by 55% and passing zero-vulnerability Trivy container scans.
   - Automated testing, linting, security scans, and container pushes to Amazon ECR via GitHub Actions on every pull request.
   - Established end-to-end observability using structured JSON application logging, CloudWatch CPU/Memory alarms, and Amazon SNS alerts.
   ```

4. **Audit Your GitHub Profile**:
   Ensure your public GitHub account presents an engineer's portfolio:
   - **Profile README**: Add a brief introduction detailing your cloud focus, tech stack icons, and links to your capstone repository.
   - **Pinned Repositories**: Pin your `cloud-native-task-manager` repository and your `90-days-of-cloud-engineering` fork.
   - **Repository Hygiene**: Check that each repository has a clean description, descriptive topics/tags (`aws`, `terraform`, `docker`, `python`), a clear README with architecture diagrams, and a permissive open-source license (MIT).

5. **Update LinkedIn Headline and Summary**:
   - **Headline**: `Junior Cloud Engineer | AWS, Terraform, Docker, Python, CI/CD`
   - **About Section**: Summarize your journey, passion for automation, hands-on experience building multi-tier AWS architectures with Terraform, and link to your GitHub.

## Done When
- [ ] Technical skills matrix organized into cloud, IaC, containers, CI/CD, and networking.
- [ ] Capstone project written out using the XYZ formula with metrics and tool mentions.
- [ ] Resume formatted cleanly as a 1-page PDF (single column, ATS-friendly text).
- [ ] GitHub profile updated with pinned repositories and README.

## Cost and Cleanup
Expected Cost: **$0.00 — no cloud resources used.**

Resume drafting and GitHub profile updates are completely free.

## Stretch Goal
Deploy your resume as a static HTML/CSS single-page application hosted on Amazon S3 with HTTPS enabled via Amazon CloudFront and a custom domain via Route 53 (the core of the Cloud Resume Challenge).

## Common Mistakes
- **Listing technologies you cannot talk about**: If you list Kubernetes or Terraform on your resume, you must be prepared to answer interview questions about pod networking or state locks. Only list what you have built with.
- **Using complex multi-column graphic templates**: Graphic-heavy resumes with skill bars (e.g. "Python: 80%") fail Applicant Tracking System (ATS) parsers. Use clean, single-column, plain text or simple markdown-to-PDF formatting.
- **Omitting GitHub links or having empty repositories**: Employers want proof of code. A link to an active GitHub repository with clear commit messages and READMEs sets you apart from 90% of applicants.

# Day 94: Interview Preparation
[← Previous Day](../day-93-cloud-resume/README.md) | [Next Day →](../day-95-whats-next/README.md)

## Goal
Prepare for cloud engineering technical interviews by mastering common architectural questions, behavioral scenarios using the STAR method, and live troubleshooting frameworks.

## Time
⏱️ Approximately 75 minutes

## Learn
- 📖 [AWS Interview Questions & Architecture Patterns](https://aws.amazon.com/architecture/) — Official architecture whitepapers and patterns commonly evaluated in technical interviews.
- 📖 [The STAR Method for Behavioral Interviews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Situation,_task,_action_and_result) — Structured behavioral interviewing technique (Situation, Task, Action, Result).

## Do
In today's career prep milestone, you will practice answering the 10 most common junior cloud engineering technical questions, prepare your behavioral STAR stories, and practice a systematic 5-step troubleshooting methodology.

1. **Master the Top 10 Technical Cloud Interview Questions**:
   Review and write concise verbal answers for each of these foundational questions:
   1. *What happens under the hood from the moment you type a URL into your browser until the page renders?* (DNS resolution, TCP 3-way handshake, TLS negotiation, HTTP request routing through CDN/ALB, web server response).
   2. *What is the difference between a Security Group and a Network ACL (NACL)?* (Security Groups are stateful and operate at the ENI instance level; NACLs are stateless and operate at the subnet boundary).
   3. *Why do we use private subnets for application servers and databases?* (Isolation from direct internet routing; ingress is only allowed through load balancers or bastion hosts, egress via NAT).
   4. *What problem does Terraform remote state locking solve?* (Prevents concurrent executions from corrupting the `.tfstate` file when multiple engineers or CI/CD pipelines run `apply`).
   5. *What is the difference between an ECS Task Execution Role and an ECS Task Role?* (Execution role is for the ECS agent to fetch ECR images and post CloudWatch logs; Task role is for the application container itself to access AWS services).
   6. *How does Docker container networking work when exposed on a host?* (Port mapping via iptables rules routes traffic from the host network namespace to the container's virtual bridge interface).
   7. *What is a multi-stage Docker build and why is it critical?* (Separates build dependencies/compilers from runtime environments, resulting in smaller, more secure production images).
   8. *How do you prevent hardcoding secrets into Git or container images?* (Use AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store; inject at runtime via environment variables or secret volumes; run pre-commit secret scanners like Trivy).
   9. *What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?* (Vertical is resizing CPU/RAM of an existing instance; horizontal is adding more instances behind a load balancer).
   10. *If your application container crashes on launch in ECS or Kubernetes, how do you troubleshoot?* (Inspect container exit code, check orchestrator event logs, review stdout/stderr in CloudWatch or `kubectl logs`, verify health check endpoint, confirm database connectivity and environment variables).

2. **Structure 3 Core Behavioral Stories Using STAR**:
   Every interview asks behavioral questions ("Tell me about a time when..."). Format your experiences using **Situation, Task, Action, Result**:
   - **Story 1: Overcoming a Technical Roadblock (Debugging/Troubleshooting)**
     - *Situation*: While setting up private subnets, my ECS containers failed to pull Docker images from ECR.
     - *Task*: Identify why the tasks were failing to initialize in private subnets.
     - *Action*: Inspected CloudWatch logs and VPC route tables. Realized private subnets lacked either a NAT Gateway or VPC Endpoints for ECR. Added VPC endpoints for ECR and S3 using Terraform.
     - *Result*: Tasks pulled images successfully with zero exposure to public internet, improving security posture and saving NAT bandwidth costs.
   - **Story 2: Managing Trade-offs (Security vs. Delivery Speed)**
   - **Story 3: Learning a Complex Tool from Scratch (Terraform / Docker)**

3. **Practice the 5-Step System Troubleshooting Framework**:
   When given an open-ended troubleshooting scenario during an interview ("A customer reports the site is throwing 500 errors. What do you do?"), follow this structured approach:
   1. **Scope the Problem**: Who is affected? All users or a subset? When did it start? Was there a recent deployment?
   2. **Inspect the Edge / Entry Point**: Check DNS resolution, CDN status, and ALB metric graphs (HTTP 502 vs 504 vs 500).
   3. **Check Application Compute & Logs**: Look at container health checks, CPU/memory usage, and CloudWatch application logs for unhandled exceptions or stack traces.
   4. **Inspect Downstream Dependencies**: Is the database reachable? Are connection pools exhausted? Are third-party APIs failing or throttling?
   5. **Remediate and Post-Mortem**: Roll back the latest release if necessary, apply hotfix, confirm metrics normalize, and document root cause analysis (RCA).

4. **Prepare Questions to Ask the Interviewer**:
   Always have 3 thoughtful questions ready:
   - "How does your engineering team manage infrastructure changes across environments—are all changes strictly gated through CI/CD pipelines?"
   - "What observability and alerting tools does your team rely on most during active incident response?"
   - "What does success look like in the first 90 days for a junior cloud engineer on this team?"

## Done When
- [ ] Prepared verbal explanations for all 10 technical questions.
- [ ] Drafted 3 STAR behavioral stories based on your curriculum labs and capstone project.
- [ ] Rehearsed the 5-step troubleshooting framework out loud.
- [ ] Prepared 3 insightful questions for hiring managers.

## Cost and Cleanup
Expected Cost: **$0.00 — no cloud resources used.**

Interview preparation is completely free.

## Stretch Goal
Conduct a 30-minute mock technical interview with a peer, mentor, or study partner from a cloud community, asking each other the technical questions and giving constructive feedback.

## Common Mistakes
- **Guessing or making up answers when you don't know**: If you don't know a specific AWS service parameter or edge case, say: *"I haven't worked directly with that specific feature yet, but based on how service X works, I would approach it by doing Y and checking the official docs."* Interviewers value honest problem-solving over fabricated answers.
- **Diving into troubleshooting without asking clarifying questions**: Jumping straight into answers without clarifying scope shows a lack of systematic thinking. Always ask clarifying questions first.
- **Focusing on the team rather than "I" in STAR stories**: Interviewers want to know what *you* did. Say "I investigated the route table and implemented the fix" rather than "We fixed it."
